SK3044 The field is guarded on some paths and not others

A private field is written without the type's one lock, and is accessed under that lock at least twice elsewhere.

CategoryAsync
Default severitywarning
ScopeCompilation
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileno — it reads the whole compilation
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
ReSharperInconsistentlySynchronizedField (resharper_inconsistently_synchronized_field_highlighting)

Why

A field taken under a lock in nine places and written bare in the tenth is a race that testing will not find: the tenth path is usually the one added last and the window is usually nanoseconds wide. The analysis is which lock, if any, is held at each access — the same analysis SK3043 needs, computed across the whole type rather than one file.

Example

Instead of:

sealed class Registry {
    readonly object gate = new();

    int count;

    public void Add() {
        lock (gate) {
            count++;
        }
    }

    public int Read() {
        lock (gate) {
            return count;
        }
    }

    public void Reset() {
        count = 0;
    }
}

Write:

sealed class Registry {
    readonly object gate = new();

    int count;

    public void Add() {
        lock (gate) {
            count++;
        }
    }

    public int Read() {
        lock (gate) {
            return count;
        }
    }

    public void Reset() {
        lock (gate) {
            count = 0;
        }
    }
}

When it does not fire

⚠ Fixless. Wrapping the offending statement in the lock is one repair and taking the lock at the caller is another, and which one is right depends on what else the caller does between the two — an edit that guesses can introduce a nested lock or a lock held across an I/O call. ⚠ The rule is deliberately far narrower than its title, and the gates are the rule. docs/plan/16 § R3: a wrong concurrency finding sends somebody to read threading code that was correct, which is the most expensive reading there is, so every gate below buys precision at the cost of recall knowingly. (1) The type must have exactly one lock object and every lock in it must be taken over that one field; two gates is a hierarchy and which one guards a given field is not decidable from the shape. (2) The type must use no other synchronization at all — no Interlocked, Volatile, Monitor, semaphore, reader-writer lock or Lazy — because any of those is ordering the rule cannot see and would call an access unguarded. That list is matched on the written name, which is right here for once: it can only silence the rule, so a collision with somebody's own Monitor costs a finding and never produces a wrong one. (3) The unguarded access must be a write. A bare read of an otherwise-guarded field is a real hazard and is also the shape of a deliberate best-effort snapshot — public int Count => count; — and the two are not distinguishable here. (4) The write must sit in a member that is callable from outside the type and that the type never calls from inside the lock; a private helper, or a public method the type itself only invokes while holding the lock, is the "caller holds the lock" contract and is extremely common. Dispose is excluded by name, because disposal after the last user has let go is the normal contract. (5) Any access to the field inside a lambda or a local function withdraws the field entirely: a delegate runs whenever somebody invokes it, holding whatever they hold. (6) At least two guarded accesses are required — one guarded and one bare is as likely to be a lock introduced in the wrong place as one forgotten in the other. ⚠ Silence is not a claim. A field this rule says nothing about is a field it could not decide, not a field it believes is synchronized.
